newsitem.title: CUBA: Blacklisted Canadian firm to hold meeting in Cuba.
newsitem.headline: Blacklisted Canadian firm to hold meeting in Cuba.

text.p: Directors of Canada's Sherritt International Corp., one of the main foreign investors in Cuba targeted by U.S. sanctions, plans to hold a board meeting on the Communist-ruled island Friday.

Patrice Merrin Best, Sherritt's vice president for corporate affairs, said the meeting in Havana would involve seven of the directors and officers who were barred from entry into the United States by U.S. authorities in July.
"All of the directors will be present and accounted for," Merrin Best said in a telephone interview Wednesday.
It will be the first time Sherritt holds a board meeting in Cuba, where the company has investments in nickel mining, oil exploration, tourism and agriculture.
The Havana meeting was a further sign that the Canadian company was determined to withstand heavy pressure from the U.S. government for it to disinvest from Cuba.

Besides Sherritt Chairman Ian Delaney, the meeting will be attended by two prominent British businessmen who are on the Sherritt board -- Rupert Pennant-Rea, a former deputy governor of the Bank of England, and Sir Patrick Sheehy, former chairman of B.A.T Industries Plc.

Those three executives were banned from entering the United States under Title IV of the so-called Helms-Burton law that was enacted in March. Sherritt was the first foreign firm in Cuba to be targeted by provisions of the law.

The law seeks to tighten the longstanding U.S. economic embargo against Cuba by penalising foreign companies and their executives who "traffick" in expropriated properties and assets in Cuba that were formerly owned by U.S. nationals or Cubans who later took U.S. citizenship.
Merrin Best described the Havana meeting as "routine" but said she was aware that the U.S. authorities might view it as further evidence of the company's business links with Cuba.
The meeting would review the company's Cuban operations, hear auditors' reports and discuss the overall business environment.
Delaney has said in the past that Sherritt is considering expanding its business in Cuba to include areas like transportation, communications and finance.
Sherritt's investments in Cuba, estimated at more than $200 million, have made the firm one of the most prominent investors on the island.

But Sherritt's joint venture in the Cuban nickel industry faces claims from former U.S. owners of a nickel plant and nickel ore reserves who operated on the island before the nationalisations that followed the 1959 Cuban Revolution.
U.S. allies such as Canada and Britain fiercely oppose the Helms-Burton law and have strongly protested the U.S. entry bans on the Sherritt executives.
U.S. authorities have also barred the executives of a Mexican telecommunications concern, Grupo Domos, which has a telephone joint venture in Cuba.
